canberra.title: ‘Spectacular’ discovery of Googong koala raises hope of local comeback
canberra.snippet: A surprise find on a walk through a Googong property has renewed hope that a koala population is living locally – and spurred a pus...
canberra.content:
29 August 2026

Start the conversation

An unexpected koala sighting has raised hopes there could be more of the much-loved marsupial in the area. Photo: Wandiyali Restoration Trust.

A surprise find on a walk through a Googong property has renewed hope that a koala population is living locally – and spurred a push to protect their habitat.

Wandiyali~Environa Wildlife Sanctuary, in southern NSW, protects a 300-hectare area of critically endangered box gum grassy woodland habitat.

It’s home to a range of threatened species, including the Speckled Warbler, Pink-tailed Worm Lizard and Gang-gang Cockatoo – and, it seems, at least one koala.

According to the listing on citizen science project NatureMapr, a sighting was logged earlier this month, before a moderator confirmed it the following day.

Carolyn Larcombe told Region that the “incredible” find was made by one of the property’s rangers.

“It’s such an amazing Australian animal that we never thought we would see here,” she said.

“Maybe the sanctuary that we’ve created here is enough of a haven to support some, which would be pretty amazing.”

But it’s not the first time the marsupial has been found on the property, following an early 2026 sighting.

That furry visitor was caught on a camera, walking along the ground near the property’s boundary.

Ms Larcombe said that was the first time they’d seen the animal “in person, so to speak”.

She believes more than one koala is making a home in the region.

“It seems a bit smaller … We think its nose is a little bit different,” she said of the recent visitor.

Another koala was also seen in the Canberra suburb of Theodore earlier this year, almost 12 months after a dead koala was found in Taylor in October 2025.

Ms Larcombe said the find had given the Wandiyali team confidence that their conservation efforts are working.

“I’ll probably be looking up more than I used to, rather than looking down at where I’m walking!” she said.

“One thing that it’s really taught us is that they’re really hard to see … Maybe we’ve had them here and we’ve just not seen.

“Maybe we’ve got this incredible safe haven [or] the animals are moving through this area.”

Koalas are listed as an endangered species in NSW and the ACT.

Ms Larcombe feels the find demonstrates the importance of protecting wildlife through “really critical” steps, suggesting that developers plant corridors to make sure there’s a pathway for wildlife to move around.

Asked whether the find showed a need to balance development with conservation, she says it “obviously” did.

“We’re very fortunate to have a beautiful patch here that we’re looking after … My brothers and I grew up here,” she said.

“I’ve got a very long connection with this land here, and one of our interests has always been biodiversity conservation and restoration.”

Ms Larcombe said dedicated conservation spaces also had another use — they helped educate people.

“I think that what it shows also is that you can have these various styles of development side by side, like in Canberra with Mulligans Flat [a conservation area].

“We’ve got a similar set-up here to Mulligans. They become these really important habitats, really important safe havens.

“But they also become these really important places that people can visit.”

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Who pays to charge the car? Canberra apartment blocks grapple with the EV question
canberra.snippet: A resident in a Canberra apartment complex had been plugging their electric vehicle into a common-area outlet, effectively sharing the el...
canberra.content:
Who should pay for the charge and the charger isn’t an easy question. Photo: James Coleman.

A resident in a Canberra apartment complex had been plugging their electric vehicle into a common-area outlet, effectively sharing the electricity bill with everyone in the building.

Other residents noticed. Complaints followed, and eventually the body corporate pulled the plug.

But that solved only one problem and created a much bigger question: as more Canberrans buy electric vehicles, who should pay to make apartment buildings ready to charge them?

The issue recently sparked a lively discussion in a Canberra community group after a resident said their owners corporation was now considering installing a proper communal EV charger.

The resident stressed they were hardly anti-EV – they hoped to own one themselves one day – but questioned why people without electric cars should contribute towards infrastructure predominantly used by those who had them.

“If the EV owner wants the convenience, the installation and associated costs should be covered by the owner,” the resident argued, also questioning whether scarce visitor parking should be given over to charging bays.

Canberrans, it turns out, have plenty of opinions on the matter.

Some community members firmly backed a user-pays approach. One said owners in their complex could install chargers in their allocated parking spaces at their own expense. Another argued it was unfair to expect the body corporate to pay for installation and maintenance.

Others saw a communal charger more like a gym or another shared facility – something not everybody uses, but which can add value to the building.

And several Canberra complexes appear to have already found a middle ground: share the cost of getting the infrastructure in place, but make EV drivers pay for the electricity they use.

One resident said their building had operated that way successfully for three years. Another said chargers had been installed in common-area bays with individual users paying for their power.

At another complex, technology has even taken care of the potentially awkward question of whose turn it is. Residents book a charging bay through an app and pay individually.

“This system works very well,” the resident said.

So, if Canberra apartment dwellers are already trying everything from private chargers to communal bays, which model is winning?

There isn’t one.

Alex Boundy, general manager – facilities at Civium, said the answer often depended on the building and how many residents actually owned EVs.

Some owners corporations fund common infrastructure. Elsewhere, individual owners pay to install chargers in their own allocated spaces. A third option splits the bill: the owners corporation pays for the electrical “backbone”, while residents pay for the equipment needed to connect their own parking spaces.

Mr Boundy said when an individual owner funded a charger, it was installed in their allocated parking space.

For buildings where interest was starting to grow, he said the sensible first step was to work out what was technically possible, take the options to owners and gauge demand before spending money.

And the communal charger may not necessarily be the future many imagine.

Mr Boundy said shared chargers were becoming less common as EV owners increasingly used slower “trickle top-up charging” at their own parking spaces rather than relying on a small number of common chargers.

What is becoming more common is the conversation itself.

“The demand is linked to EV ownership uptake which is on the up, partnered with more Canberrans living in apartments than previously,” Mr Boundy said.

“It certainly is par for the course now with regard to talking vehicle charging within apartment buildings.”

Is it as simple as finding a spare outlet? Hardly. While that initial shared-socket approach offered an easy fix, building power is not a free-for-all resource.

An ACT Government spokesperson said those power points are managed by the owners corporation under the Unit Titles (Management) Act, and corporations can introduce rules governing their use.

That doesn’t necessarily mean an existing outlet is off limits forever. Devices are available that can measure how much electricity a resident uses and ensure they pay their share – potentially removing one of the biggest causes of neighbourly irritation.

Installing a dedicated charger requires another step.

Whether it is going into an owner’s parking space or onto common property, the installation must be approved by the owners corporation through a special resolution. The government says that permission cannot be unreasonably withheld.

If the charger is connected to the building’s common electricity meter, there should also be a mechanism for the EV owner to repay the corporation for the electricity they consume.

The bigger challenge is avoiding a situation in which every new EV owner arrives with a different proposal, leaving the building with a patchwork of chargers and electrical connections.

The ACT Government is instead encouraging apartment buildings to think ahead and become “EV ready”. In simple terms, that means installing the shared electrical backbone needed to reach every apartment’s parking space. Residents can then add and pay for their own charger when they eventually buy an EV.

For new Canberra apartments, some of that future planning is already built in. Since September 2024, new multi-unit developments have been required to provide EV-ready infrastructure to every residential unit’s car space.

Older buildings face the harder task of retrofitting infrastructure that was never designed to accommodate dozens of cars plugging in overnight.

“Owners corporations can seek free building-specific advice through the ACT Government’s Sustainable Apartments Program, while interest-free loans for EV-ready infrastructure have also been announced and are due to launch,” the spokesperson added.

Which brings the debate neatly back to where it began: one car, one communal power point and a few neighbours wondering why they were helping pay the bill.

The extension cord may have been unplugged, but the question it sparked isn’t going away.

As more Canberrans switch to EVs – and more call apartments home – body corporates will increasingly have to decide whether charging infrastructure is a private convenience or simply the next thing a modern apartment building needs to be ready for.

canberra.title: Dumpling Social expands north with a new Braddon venue
canberra.snippet: Dumpling Social has opened a second location on Lonsdale Street, bringing its colourful casual take on modern Chinese dining to one of Ca...
canberra.content:
Buns taste like the offspring of a dumpling and a pizza. Photo: Sophia Brady.

Dumpling Social has opened a second location on Lonsdale Street, bringing its colourful casual take on modern Chinese dining to one of Canberra’s most iconic dining strips.

I first visited Dumpling Social when it opened in Woden in 2020, drawn in by the promise of soup-filled dumplings and clever takes on familiar favourites. While the dumplings remain a drawcard, a recent visit to the new Braddon restaurant revealed plenty of reasons to look beyond the bamboo steamer.

From the street, a small window gives a glimpse of dumplings being folded by hand. Step inside and the venue opens into a surprisingly large space. Clean lines, timber tables and warm lighting set the mood, while the dining room seems to keep stretching further back the deeper you venture inside.

The restaurant is fully licensed, with beer, wine, sake and soju available alongside cocktails and a mocktail list. We started with two of the alcohol-free options, both arriving in bright shades that showed the venue’s fondness for all things vibrant.

The Watermelon Mojito leaned heavily into sweet flavours, edging close to dessert territory. The Sakura Blossom was a pretty drink that combined the light floral notes of rose with cherry blossom, lychee, lemon and soda.

The food menu is divided into sections including starters, smaller plates, dumplings, raw plates, larger dishes, rice and noodles, and desserts. One useful thing to know before visiting is that dishes arrive as they are prepared rather than in a fixed order. Everything reaches the table quickly. If you want a slower progression through the menu, order a few dishes at a time.

The Yellowfin Tuna Carpaccio is more substantial than it appears. Photo: Sophia Brady.

The Braised Pork Belly Bao was the first dish to arrive. Do you remember, there was a period when bao buns appeared on almost every menu in town. This dish reminds you why they became so popular in the first place. The soft, cloud-like bun held slow-braised pork belly glazed in house char siu sauce alongside crunchy pickled wombok. Sticky, rich and slightly tangy, proving bao buns are still very good.

From the raw plates section, the Yellowfin Tuna Carpaccio offered a lighter counterpoint. The thick slices of tuna sat in a shallow pool of spiced orange vinaigrette, making the dish feel surprisingly substantial. A gentle hit of Tabasco added warmth.

Then there are the dumplings.

First came the Pan Fried Prawn and Cheese Bun. Served with a warning about the hot liquid and melted cheese inside, these soft yeast buns are filled with pork, prawn, mozzarella, and a little broth. They tasted like the offspring of a dumpling and a pizza. They are delightful to pop into your mouth, totally unexpected and very moreish.

The Pan-Fried Beef and Onion Dumplings offered a more traditional option. Green in colour and nicely crispy on the bottom, it was loaded with filling; the beef was bold and assertive.

Old Town Twice Cooked Sticky Pork Belly. Photo: Sophia Brady.

The star of the larger dishes was the Old Town Twice Cooked Sticky Pork Belly. Large chunks of pork arrived coated in a glossy ginger-caramel and palm-sugar sauce with the consistency of golden syrup. The caramelised edges and soft rendered fat soaked up every bit of that sticky sauce, producing a dish that lived up to its name.

Dumpling Social adds something a little different to the Lonsdale Street mix. The playful combinations and the colourful dishes arriving across the table make this new location a fun visit.

Dumpling Social is located at 10 Lonsdale St, Braddon, and is open for lunch and dinner 7 days a week from 11:30 am.

canberra.title: Pokemon cards are the modern day gold rush and Canberra is the mine!
canberra.snippet: As demand and prices soar for Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering, and Yu-Gi-Oh! cards, some collectors are turning trading into a full-time ca...
canberra.content:
Collect-A-Verse is becoming one of the fastest-growing card trading events in the country. Photo: Collect-A-Verse.

As demand and prices soar for Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering, and Yu-Gi-Oh! cards, some collectors are turning trading into a full-time career.

That is no different for collectors here in Canberra, who sell thousands of cards each year for thousands of dollars.

The thrill of unpacking and selling cards has taken the ACT by storm, so much so that the ACT now hosts one of the biggest regular trading events in the country: Collect-A-Verse.

So what makes a few square centimetres of cardboard with an illustration so valuable, and why are so many people so in on the fad?

Collect-A-Verse organiser Dan Rathbone said trading card popularity has picked up dramatically in the last 12 months, with record prices being set around the world.

Mr Rathbone said he believes a big part of it comes from nostalgia, with kids who enjoyed the likes of Pokémon as children in the 90s and early 2000s now having ‘adult money’.

“Prices have skyrocketed, and it’s just been this wave of people wanting to invest in something that they had as a kid,” he said.

“We’re seeing Pikachus and Charizards from Pokémon selling for hundreds of thousands of dollars. The singer Post Malone bought a Magic: The Gathering card featuring The One Ring from The Lord of the Rings for over US$2 million.

“It has really become an industry of its own.”

The price of trading cards isn’t the only thing growing either. So far, Mr Rathbone and the team at Geek Events have held two previous Collect-A-Verse events in 2026.

The first was at the University of Canberra in January, the second at Thoroughbred Park in June and the next is scheduled for Exhibition Park on 5 September.

Mr Rathbone said the first event saw about 25 vendors offer to sell their cards, but now their September event has more than doubled, with over 50 vendors expected to attend.

“We are in that perfect spot between Melbourne and Sydney,” he said.

“There are so many people between those cities who collect and buy cards, and it’s expanding to the regions as well.

“Canberra is a great spot for people in those regional areas to come in and see what’s on offer without driving five-plus hours to the other big cities.”

Mr Rathbone said the next event in September will have something for every collector’s budget, with cards priced as low as 50 cents and as high as $70,000.

“We’ve had some high-graded hooded Pikachus sell for over $10,000,” he said.

“At one stage, we had a couple of Pikachu cards where they look like Mario and Luigi that were up for sale for around $73,000, last we checked.

“With that said, not everything will be that expensive. There are plenty of opportunities for people to buy and see something they like without breaking the bank.

“That’s part of the fun with trading cards. Sometimes it’s the cards that are worth just a dollar that mean the most.”

The next Collect-A-Verse meeting will be held at Exhibition Park on Saturday, 5 September, from 9 am to 4 pm. Tickets are required before 2 pm; entry after 2 pm is free. To purchase tickets, visit Humanitix.

canberra.title: ‘Too great a risk’: Accused bikie boss refused bail over alleged cocaine trafficking
canberra.snippet: A magistrate has said she has “no faith whatsoever” that an accused bikie boss would follow any conditions if released on bai...
canberra.content:
Matthew William Byrne will next face court in September. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A magistrate has said she has “no faith whatsoever” that an accused bikie boss would follow any conditions if released on bail.

On Friday (28 August), an ACT Policing spokesperson said the Criminal Investigations Drug and Organised Crime Team began investigating an alleged criminal group in early 2025.

“Police will allege the group has been involved in the trafficking of more than 70 kilograms of cocaine, with an estimated street value exceeding $10 million,” they said.

About 5:30 pm on Thursday (27 August), officers carried out a traffic stop on a white Toyota LandCruiser in Lyneham and arrested a 36-year-old man wanted in connection with the investigation.

Officers searched the man’s vehicle and seized several items, including two phones, a laptop and computer, gemstones, four vintage glass-sealed comic books and more than $1200 in cash.

Police also seized the LandCruiser.

It’s also alleged the man had a ledger containing assets owned by the man and liabilities totalling more than $3.3 million.

During a later search of the man’s Yarralumla residence, the spokesperson said police also located and seized a number of vials (believed to contain anabolic steroids), an extendable baton and a white Volkswagen Golf.

When Matthew William Byrne faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Friday, the court heard that he is accused of being a leader of the group.

He has been charged with being part of a criminal group, recruiting others to assist in a criminal activity, trafficking in a commercial quantity of cocaine and possessing a prohibited weapon.

Mr Byrne’s defence lawyer described an alleged connection between Mr Byrne and the gang as “somewhat tenuous”.

He said his client had no connection with alleged “drug runners”. He said while Mr Byrne was discovered with steroids, that was because he’s “obviously going to the gym”.

He said that, despite carrying out a long-term operation, police did not act against Mr Byrne over concerns he was allegedly offending before Thursday (27 August).

“If they thought there was a serious question about him engaging in serious criminal conduct in May 2025, they would have acted on it,” he said.

“They didn’t … none of this was brought to the court’s attention [at that time].”

He said his client, if released, was willing to follow “stringent” bail conditions that would place him under effective house arrest.

However, the prosecutor said the proposed bail conditions “mirror, in parts” the court orders previously placed on Mr Byrne, when he was subject to an intensive correction order (ICO).

She alleged those restrictions — as well as family support — had not stopped Mr Byrne from further offending.

”The circumstances that are before Your Honour … are, with respect, exactly the same [as in previous proceedings],” she said.

“The accused received the benefit of those matters on that occasion, and it has not … dissuaded him from continuing in offending on an ongoing basis.”

She also alleged that Mr Byrne used encrypted services to communicate with others, in breach of those orders.

“[It’s alleged he gave] phones to those persons and directed them to use those encrypted services, and directed them with respect to behaviour that would reduce the likelihood of their criminal activities coming to light,” she said of the allegations.

“For example, leaving devices at the border with the ACT and NSW.”

The prosecutor said police intelligence indicated Mr Byrne was the figure allegedly referred to as “boss or old mate” in messages allegedly intercepted by police.

“The prosecution position is that, at this point in time, this is not a weak case.”

Special Magistrate Lucinda Wilson ultimately refused Mr Byrne’s bail and found he represented “too great a risk” to the community if released on bail.

“The court has no faith whatsoever that any bail conditions, no matter how harsh, would be complied with by you,” she said.

“What is alleged is extremely serious offending — and not only is it extremely serious offending, it is very similar to the offending that you were caught doing in August, September, October 2022 and pleaded guilty to.”

Mr Byrne will next face court on 11 September. No pleas were entered.

Earlier this week, two alleged co-offenders — 36-year-old Adam Ha and 31-year-old Domenico Luca Costanzo — faced the ACT Magistrates Court.

Both men have pleaded not guilty to their charges and will return to court in October and September, respectively.

australia.title: Statins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial shows
australia.snippet: Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older people Taking...
australia.content:
Taking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.

Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having a major heart event such as a heart attack, stroke, or from requiring heart surgery.

People who have already had a major heart event are also commonly prescribed the drugs, regardless of their age.

What doctors did not know was whether it was safe to prescribe a daily statin to people aged 70 and over who were healthy overall, having never experienced a heart attack, stroke or heart surgery, and whether doing so could prevent these cardiac events.

A co-author of the study, Adjunct Prof Mark Nelson with the Monash University school of public health and preventive medicine, said it was an important piece of missing information, because the biggest risk of major heart-related events “is increasing age”.

“Our society is ageing, and therefore the burden of disease is increasing, making it important to improve our ability to prevent disease in this group,” he said. “So we needed the evidence for this group to see if prescribing statins as a prevention measure works.”

But Nelson said older adults were often overlooked in early statin research because 40 years ago, heart disease was most common in middle-aged populations especially if they smoked, leading public health efforts to focus on preventing premature deaths in that group. Elderly populations may also be sick and on other medications, making trialling drugs risky, he said.

To address the gap, Monash researchers analysed the cardiovascular outcomes of almost 10,000 study participants over the age of 70 who were given either a daily statin or a placebo, in a scientifically-robust type of study known as a randomised control trial. The participants were enrolled with the help of almost 3,400 GPs across Australia.

The researchers excluded people who had a condition that might make taking a statin unsafe, if they were not living independently, or if they already needed the drug because they had suffered a heart attack.

The decade-long study found the medication decreased the risk of a first major cardiovascular event by 30% for those aged over 70.

In real terms, this means one major cardiac event such as a heart attack, stroke, or heart surgery could be prevented for every 37 older adults treated with daily statins over almost six years.

Prof James Chong, a cardiologist at Sydney’s Westmead hospital, said if the research “leads to increased statin use globally, the absolute reduction of (heart-related) events can be significant”.

“One of the major changes that may result, in my opinion, is more elderly patients having confidence to take long term statins,” he said.

“However, one thing we have to keep in mind is it was an almost exclusively white population with the mean age around 75 years of age, so the results may not be as generalisable globally without further supporting evidence.”

The findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine on Saturday and presented concurrently at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Germany.

Lead researcher on the paper, Adjunct Prof Sophia Zoungas, said: “What we hope to see, now that we have provided such strong evidence, are updated treatment guidelines to help clinicians make use of this new finding.”

Older patients should have a conversation with their GP about whether statins are appropriate to help them stay healthy, the researchers said.

Prof Tom Marwick, a cardiologist at Hobart’s Royal hospital, said there had been a lot of misinformation about statins increasing the risk of dementia, making some older people reluctant to take the drugs.

A benefit of the Monash study was that the findings “really close the book on that, in large numbers,” he said. The study found no statistically significant difference in dementia rates among those who received a statin and those who did not.

Marwick described it as a “well done, really important trial”.

But he said the study also found patients were reluctant to adhere to therapy, with more than 15% of patients in the trial discontinuing their medication.

Marwick said “a slight disappointment” in the findings was that although major heart events were reduced, the disability-free survival was the same among the participants whether they took the statin or the placebo.

In other words, taking the medication didn’t extend life or its quality.

“We can reduce cardiovascular events, but the health burdens of ageing are less amenable,” he said.

australia.title: Plug-in solar panels could save households up to $370 a year – if Australia made them legal as in the UK
australia.snippet: A plug-in solar kit that costs about $1,000 ‘pays for itself in three years’, one expert says Get our breaking news email , free app or d...
australia.content:
Millions of Australians could be saving up to $370 a year on energy bills and doing their bit for the climate crisis if Labor followed the UK’s lead in legalising plug-in solar panels, an advocacy group has said.

Plug-in solar refers to small standalone solar units that could be attached to balconies or used in back yards and plugged into power points, offsetting the energy used by household appliances.

Researchers have estimated Australians living in capital cities could save between $226 and $372 each year with a plug-in system.

While these systems are sold in Australia, they are not yet legal to plug in and use.

As a result, Heidi Lee Douglas, chief executive of Solar Citizens, said more than a third of Australians who rented or lived in apartments were missing out on the “bill-busting benefits” that solar homeowners enjoyed.

The campaign organisation has urged Australian governments to make plug-in solar available, after the technology was made legal in the United Kingdom this week, with units going on sale from Thursday.

“It’s unfair that more than three million Aussies who could benefit from portable plug-in solar panels are missing out because our regulations aren’t up to date with the latest technology,” she said.

“We see the UK, Germany, Spain and our neighbour New Zealand making plug-in solar available – so it’s time for Australian politicians and regulators to work it out here. If it’s good enough for the Kiwis and the Brits, it’s good enough for us.”

Solar and battery engineer Glen Morris, director of the Smart Energy Lab, said an 800-watt system could produce enough power to run a fridge, television and other appliances during the day.

“A kit that costs about $1,000 pays for itself in three years and keeps working for twenty,” he said. “For most renters it is the only form of solar they can own, and they take it with them when they move.”

Only about 11% of Australian renters have solar installed, compared with about 44% of homeowners, research by Energy Consumers Australia found. A similar gap existed for those living in apartments, with 6% having solar, compared with 39% of people in detached or semi-detached houses.

The consumer organisation said renters were missing out due to the “split incentive” problem, where landlords faced the upfront costs of installing solar, while tenants gained the most benefits. Apartment dwellers also faced structural barriers due to the complexities governing common property, the research found.

Along with unprecedented uptake of household solar and battery systems, the research revealed record quarterly investment in large-scale solar, with 1.8 gigawatts reaching final investment decision – the strongest result since the regulator began tracking investment activity.

The regulator’s acting chair, Carl Binning, said “the speed of the transition is accelerating”, adding that strong battery demand under the government’s Cheaper Home Batteries program had helped boost rooftop solar.

“We’ve now received more than 500,000 battery applications since the program started, which shows the scale of household demand when the economics stack up,” he said.

australia.title: What we know about the Australians missing in the Nepal floods
australia.snippet: More than 40 Australians are among several thousand people unaccounted for after catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border How the ...
australia.content:
An 11-year-old child, an ADF member and many other pilgrims and trekkers have been named among the Australians missing after deadly flash floods and landslides tore through valleys on the Nepal-Tibet border.

As of Saturday there were 41 Australians among almost 2,500 people reported missing in the disaster, including at least 777 foreigners. At least 93,000 people were estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.

Here’s what we know about the Australians who remain missing. This article will be updated as more information becomes available.

australia.title: Another beloved live music venue is closing. Is Australia’s precarious rental market killing the vibe?
australia.snippet: With Lazy Thinking in Sydney the latest venue to shut its doors, the once-vibrant grassroots music scene is becoming increasingly vulnera...
australia.content:
Jim Flanagan has four days to hand his keys back to his landlord.

Panels engulfed in grungy band posters, handmade plates that have served countless customers, a shelving unit housing a library of iconic vinyls: all of it will be sold for next to nothing in the rush to vacate.

But not before Lazy Thinking hosts one final, family affair: a farewell gig on Saturday night.

The not-for-profit music venue has been forced to close its doors in Dulwich Hill, in Sydney’s inner west, after it was asked to vacate by the landlord, according to Flanagan.

It is the latest in a spate of live music venue closures that is fuelling calls to re-examine the influence landlords exert over Australia’s culture and nightlife.

Flanagan says Lazy Thinking had been on a month-by-month lease for years, but after starting a conversation with the landlords about the building’s infrastructure and a long-term lease, it became clear they “weren’t interested in arriving at a productive solution”.

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

Though disappointed, Flanagan says the issue is systemic among arts and live music venues.

“The obsession with property ownership means that live music venues are always exposed as commercial renters … They are very often at risk to both the political and economic whims of the marketplace,” he says.

“You are overwhelmingly talking about businesses that are renting their properties, and we have some of the lowest rental protections in the developed world – all of those forces mean landlords exercise a profound influence over our arts sector.”

The Bearded Lady in Brisbane’s West End closed in May 2025 after negotiations with the venue’s landlord fell through, The Jade in central Adelaide in January announced its closure after its venue’s lease was not renewed and in March last year the Gasometer hotel in Melbourne’s Collingwood ended operations after its building owners rejected offers for another party to take over the business, organisers said.

In July, LGBTQ+ inclusive performing arts venue Divine Playhouse was booted from a deconsecrated church in the Sydney CBD over what its landlord, Redevelop, deemed to be “offensive trade”.

A host of other live music venues including MoshPit, Darling Nikki’s and Mary’s Underground – all in Sydney – and Melbourne’s Stay Gold, Bendigo hotel and Misfits have also announced their closures since the beginning of 2026.

While most have cited financial pressures rather than interactions with landlords, being a renter can add to economic burden. Venue operators are often pincered between rising rents and disappearing income streams – particularly the loss of revenue from ever-declining alcohol sales.

Aran Tanaka Van de Ven, a venue manager for the group that operated Stay Gold, has worked at spaces with lease clauses stipulating rent can never go backwards.

“Live music venues are often a labour of love,” he says. “But for landlords, the value of their property has always got to be protected, even if it’s in a climate where everyone’s business is devalued because there’s a cost-of-living crisis.”

After engaging with almost 100 venues, music industry figures and stakeholders across Europe, the RMIT University live music venue expert Dr Sam Whiting found owning the building in which the venue operates was fundamental to long-term sustainability.

“Venues often rent commercial premises where the landlord doesn’t care what kind of way the building is used, they just want to make sure that their rent is paid on time and the lease is fulfilled,” Whiting says.

“So music venues don’t have security of tenure, which means a lack of certainty, which breeds unease and precariousness.”

Those owned by the operators were able to plan better, weather challenges more easily and apply for grants with greater success. Spaces with longer leases were also able to better forecast and plan – but private landlords were not incentivised to support this, Whiting found.

The Real Estate Institute of New South Wales chief executive officer, Tim McKibbin, says landlords are investors who want the maximum annual return and capital growth, and no harm to their asset, and warns that imposing restrictions on investors will lead them to take their funds elsewhere.

The CEO of the institute’s Victorian branch, Toby Balazs, echoes this sentiment.

“If governments want to support live music and arts venues, the focus should be on targeted incentives that encourage owners to retain and provide suitable spaces, rather than policies that penalise property owners or interfere with commercial agreements,” he says.

Many of the venues left standing are encouraged to act more like larger spaces, which book palatable artists to attract a general audience rather than catering for specific communities, the SydneyMusic co-founder Joe Hardy says.

“Everything is a venue for hire, so it will be one scene on one day and another scene another day and there’s no real continuity,” he says.

“This means the space doesn’t become an incubator for community, it is just a place where they hope to sell enough tickets and drinks over the bar.”

This curtails artists’ creative expression and, when combined with restrictions regarding sound, curfews and other limits, kills the vibe for punters.

“If you wonder why less and less people care about live music, you should look at the vibe,” the SydneyMusic co-founder Caitlin Welsh says.

Smaller venues are also integral for emerging artists, with Hacky Sack singer-songwriter Huck Hastings noting his biggest shows in 2025 followed a gig at Lazy Thinking.

“If we don’t have places to play or if we don’t see an arts career modelled for us, there’s going to be no way forward,” he says.

The NSW government has introduced a series of vibrancy reforms, including funding for venues, while its Victorian and Queensland counterparts have announced grants for spaces and local musicians.

“If we let our music venues fail then our night-time economies and our cultural life will suffer, and we can’t afford to let that happen,” the NSW music minister, John Graham, says.

But Whiting says arguments about the economic benefits of live music are not enough, particularly for smaller venues that rarely turn a profit.

Instead, he has called for governments and the industry to reorient policy towards treating live music as a public good, similar to education or health, as this would lower barriers to entry for musicians, participants and audiences.

He also recommends the establishment of community land trusts, and suggested Australia create an equivalent to the UK’s Music Venue Properties. The community-funded charity buys buildings that host grassroots music venues and leases them back to their current operators, offering affordable rents, support with repairs and insurance, and flexibility.

Governments could also buy spaces and act as benevolent landlords, or collaborate with venues to co-own spaces, Whiting says.

Tanaka Van de Ven and Flanagan support current government measures but believe more must be done to address the root causes eating away at the sector.

“The live music scene is now in utter crisis,” Flanagan says. “I’m not going to reopen the Lazy Thinking venue in anything that looks like the same setup.

“Perhaps it’s a government-provided free space, perhaps it’s a space that one of our donors provides at a discounted rent … but the new venue will have an entirely different economic framework because the existing one just doesn’t work.”

australia.title: Royal commission lays bare the fear and anger of Jewish Australians. But has it got to the heart of antisemitism?
australia.snippet: Hearings began amid the grief of the Bondi attack. The community hopes the inquiry will ‘help us to go back to the Australia that we love...
australia.content:
As the university student Liat was excused from the witness stand of the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion, she felt a weight lifted off her chest.

“It was certainly very cathartic for me … having gone through the majority of my university life in a state of fear,” she says.

Liat, who spoke publicly under her first name only due to safety concerns, had just told the commission about the “pervasive fear” that emerged on campus after Hamas’s October 7 attack and Israel’s subsequent war on Gaza.

The 22-year-old student, whose parents were both born in Israel, said she was labelled a “baby killer” and genocide supporter.

Liat was among more than 300 witnesses who testified in the royal commission, which concluded public hearings after four months this week.

It was, from the very beginning, a mammoth task with a tight deadline of less than 12 months. The work began in a moment of raw grief and anger felt by Jewish Australians in the aftermath of the Bondi terror attack, when 15 people were killed during a Hanukah celebration.

But the inquiry has also drawn criticism for the narrow definition it used to describe antisemitism, for only considering the broader context of racism in its final weeks, and for limited inclusion of Jewish Australians who have spoken in support of Palestine and been criticised for it.

But while community leaders have differing opinions on how the commission’s public hearings have fared, there is unity in the desire for solutions to stamp out the pervasiveness of antisemitism in the everyday lives of Jewish Australians.

Ordinary Jewish Australians

For Alex Ryvchin, the co-chair of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, the public hearings laid bare the anguish and safety fears of community members.

“You’ve had people who don’t ordinarily have a platform, ordinary members of the community, who’ve been called and who have given heart-rending, harrowing accounts of what it’s like every single day for an ordinary Jewish Australian,” he says.

“To me, that’s really the most important thing – for the royal commission and also for the country to hear that,” he says.

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

The final week of hearings was dominated by calls from the federal opposition and some Jewish community leaders to extend the inquiry’s timeframe to hear from more witnesses.

The calls were resisted by the commissioner, Virginia Bell SC, who has requested a short extension of the reporting deadline so the release of the final report does not coincide with the first anniversary of the Bondi attack.

The opposition frontbencher Julian Leeser, a Jewish MP, named Anthony Albanese and senior cabinet ministers including the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, among a cohort of people he said should appear before the inquiry to explain “what went wrong from the very top”.

Ryvchin is “sceptical” about what calling senior political figures would have achieved, saying “we hear enough from them”.

He says the commission has “ample” evidence to draw the “correct conclusions about what has caused this crisis, what led to Bondi and what remedies we need to improve as a country”.

“I personally feel that things have gotten even worse since Bondi. The question is: will we see the right conclusions to lead us out of it?

“Will we see those who are truly responsible for it held to account? … That’s what remains to be seen.”

Getting to the core of antisemitism?

Dr Max Kaiser, a Jewish historian who sits on the advisory committee of the Jewish Council of Australia (JCA) – a progressive advocacy group – says there were gaps in who the commission heard from.

Speaking in a personal capacity, he says the commission heard limited public testimony from Jewish Australians who have participated in pro-Palestine protests, including those charged under Queensland’s hate speech crackdown.

That means the commission failed to hear from those whose activism in support of Palestine has made them the target of abuse from pro-Israel activists, he says.

“They view that expression of solidarity with Palestinians as very much part of their Jewish values and very much about saying never again for anyone,” he says.

“It is very intensive abuse aimed at people’s Jewish identity and calling into question their Jewish identities.”

Sarah Schwartz, the JCA’s executive officer, told the commission she had been called a traitor and “Hitler’s Jew” because of her advocacy for Palestinians, in online harassment from pro-Israel and neo-Nazi groups.

Jewish leaders have also raised concerns about witnesses at the commission being subjected to online abuse after testifying.

In June, the Australian federal police charged a man with allegedly harassing a royal commission witness by sending three emails. The man was found in possession of neo-Nazi material and leaflets for the National Socialist Network – now proscribed as a hate group under Australian laws.

Asked whether the commission got to the heart of antisemitism in modern Australia, Kaiser replies that only in its final two weeks did the commission hear from experts on the importance of viewing antisemitism in the wider context of racism.

“Any commission that was seriously wanting to talk about antisemitism and understand it as a complex social issue and understand it at its root cause needed to start from examining antisemitism as a form of racism and understanding the wider international and Australian context,” he says.

He also criticised the lack of experts who could challenge the commission’s use of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism as a guiding framework during the inquiry.

The definition, which has been adopted by the federal government, is accompanied by illustrative examples, which opponents have argued means it can be used to conflate antisemitism with legitimate criticism of Israel.

Ryvchin says the commission’s recommendations will reveal whether it has gotten to the core of how antisemitism operates in Australia.

Bondi evidence behind closed doors

The public hearings have offered a narrow glimpse into the information about the Bondi terror attack before the commission.

In her closing address this week, Bell acknowledged there may be frustration that much of the evidence about the Bondi attack was heard behind closed doors but stressed the need to not prejudice the ongoing criminal proceedings.

The commission’s interim report in April found that Sydney’s Jewish community had told police of a “high” threat of an attack at the Chanukah by the Sea festival at Bondi, but that New South Wales police appeared not to have completed a comprehensive risk assessment for the event.

Nomi Kaltmann, a Jewish Australian lawyer and journalist based in Melbourne, says she hopes the necessary security protocol changes are swiftly implemented after the final report is handed down.

“No community in Australia should endure the grief and anguish that my Jewish community has endured over the past eight months,” she says.

The Sydney-based Rabbi Jacqueline Ninio leads the congregation at Woollahra’s Emanuel Synagogue – about a 10-minute drive from where the Bondi attack occurred. She says the Jewish community is still in a “deep process of grief and mourning”.

“We’re holding on to hope and belief that this royal commission can really make a difference and help us to go back to the Australia that we love,” she says.

world.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
world.snippet: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours Austrian police are hunting...
world.content:
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.

The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”

Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.

MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.

Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.

The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.

A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.

European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.

In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.

This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.

A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.

world.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
world.snippet: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands ...
world.content:
In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.

Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.

Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”

It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.

In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”

The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.

That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

world.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
world.snippet: Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime The UK Foreign Offic...
world.content:
The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.

Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.

Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.

Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.

“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.

Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.

But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”

Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.

Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.

The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.

On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.

Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.

Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.

The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

world.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
world.snippet: Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking South African police h...
world.content:
South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.

A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.

The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.

Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.

The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”

Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.

The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.

South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

world.title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?
world.snippet: The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly...
world.content:
A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?

Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.

What is mpox?

Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.

It used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend changing it to mpox.

It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox was on course to become endemic in the US.

Why is it spreading to new countries?

There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.

The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with men at the highest risk.

In June 2024, researchers raised the alarm about a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.

“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.

“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.

What happened to those two big outbreaks?

The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.

The 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency status lifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.

If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.

How worrying is the new outbreak?

Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.

“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.” 

However, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”  

Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”

Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.

Are there vaccines and treatments?

The WHO recommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.

Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”

A new global stockpile is due to be launched within weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.

An antiviral called tecovirimat did not appear any better than a placebo when tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.

While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.

“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”
